mainTopic: ביטול רשות in a shared חצר: who may give away courtyard rights to whom, and whether one ביטול must be made to each resident
overview: This amud continues the גמרא's discussion of ביטול רשות, where a resident who did not join the עירוב gives up his rights in a shared חצר so carrying becomes permitted on שבת. First the גמרא finishes explaining why the משנה needed to say that two may give rights to one, and why it needed to say that rights may not be received, even through 'קני על מנת להקנות.' Then אביי asks רבה whether a forgetful resident among five must give up his rights to each of the others separately, and רבה says yes. אביי challenges him from a ברייתא that lets a non-joiner give his rights 'to one who joined.' רבה answers that the second joiner died, and the two sides argue over how to read the ברייתא's clauses. The question against אביי's reading of 'to two' ends as a קשיא. The גמרא then goes through every clause of the ברייתא and explains why each one is needed according to both אביי and רבה. Finally, רבא asks רב נחמן whether an heir may do ביטול רשות, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why the משנה had to say two may give rights to one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its answer. We might have thought חז"ל should make a גזירה against two giving rights to one, in case people also start giving rights to two. The משנה teaches that no such גזירה exists.
steps.simpleTranslation: [You might have said:] Let us make a decree, lest people come to give up their rights to them (to two). So the משנה teaches us that we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to 'why did the משנה need to say that two may give their rights to one?' It explains what mistake we might otherwise have made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Giving rights to two people does not work, because two non-joiners still share the courtyard. Someone could have argued that even two-to-one should be banned so people won't confuse it with one-to-two. The משנה tells us we don't worry about that confusion, so two-to-one is fully allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us make a rabbinic decree (גזירה)
It teaches us (the new point of the source)

phrases.english: Let us decree, lest he come to renounce to them (to two).
phrases.notes: The suggested worry: people would confuse two-to-one with one-to-two.

phrases.english: It teaches us [that we do not decree].
phrases.notes: This is why the משנה needed the line.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer, begun on the previous amud, to the question of why the משנה needed its line.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the need for the משנה's wording by rejecting a possible גזירה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have banned two-to-one so people would not come to give rights to two.
steps.terutzMaskana: No גזירה is made. Two may give rights to one.

steps.title: Why does the משנה need to say rights may not be received
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'ואין נוטלין רשות' from the משנה and asks why this line is needed, since it seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And they may not receive rights.' Why do I need this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה and asks why it needs to be stated. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two residents who did not join the עירוב still share the courtyard with each other. So giving them rights clearly cannot help, and the line seems unnecessary. The גמרא wants to find the new case it teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? (the line seems unnecessary)

phrases.english: And they may not receive rights.
Why do I need this?
phrases.notes: Asking why the line is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What new case is taught by 'ואין נוטלין רשות'?

steps.title: Even 'acquire in order to pass on' does not work
steps.stepSummary: The line is needed for this case: the other residents tell one of the two non-joiners, 'Acquire our rights so that you can pass them to your friend.' Even then it does not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where they tell him: 'Acquire on condition that you transfer [it to your friend].'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The משנה is teaching a less obvious case: even a plan of 'take it and then pass it on' does not help.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We might have thought the first non-joiner could act as a middleman. He would receive the rights for a moment and then hand them to the second, leaving only one person in charge. The משנה rules that he cannot receive rights at all in this situation, so he cannot pass them on either.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a special case)
Acquire on condition that you transfer to another

steps.whatToRemember: 'ואין נוטלין רשות' teaches that a non-joiner cannot act as a middleman, even through a 'קני על מנת להקנות' arrangement.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary,
even though they say to him:
phrases.notes: The other residents speak to one of the two non-joiners.

phrases.english: Acquire on condition to transfer.
phrases.notes: Transfer to his friend, the other non-joiner.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, אַף עַל גַּב דְּאָמְרִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'למה לי' of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a special case (לא צריכא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A non-joiner could receive rights in order to pass them to his friend.
steps.terutzMaskana: He cannot receive them even for passing on.

steps.title: Must a forgetful resident renounce to each person separately
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבה about five residents sharing a courtyard, where one forgot to join the עירוב. When he gives up his rights, must he do so to each of the other four separately?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי asked רבה: Five people live in one courtyard, and one of them forgot and did not join the עירוב. When he renounces his rights, must he renounce to each and every one, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic opens. אביי asks רבה a practical question about how ביטול רשות must be done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether giving up rights works like a gift to each person, so each one needs it directly. The other option is that one general renunciation covers everyone. This is a question about the technical form of ביטול.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him (a question of the student to the teacher)

phrases.english: Abaye asked Rabba:
Five who live in one courtyard,
and one of them forgot and did not join the eiruv,
when he renounces his rights,
must he renounce to each and every one
or not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new inquiry about how ביטול רשות is done.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does ביטול רשות have to be made to each resident separately?

steps.title: רבה: he must renounce to each one
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the forgetful resident must give up his rights to each and every resident.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He must renounce to each and every one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a clear answer to אביי's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבה, a single general renunciation is not enough. Each of the other residents must receive it. The next step challenges this ruling.

phrases.english: He said to him:
He must renounce to each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: צָרִיךְ לְבַטֵּל לְכׇל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, he must renounce to each resident separately.

steps.title: אביי challenges from a ברייתא about giving rights to one
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes a ברייתא. It lists who may give rights to whom, including a non-joiner giving his rights to 'one who joined.' This suggests that giving to a single person is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: He objected: One who did not join may give his rights to one who joined. Two who joined may give their rights to one who did not join. Two who did not join may give their rights to two who joined, or to one who did not join.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבה's answer using a ברייתא. The next step finishes quoting the ברייתא, and steps 8-9 spell out the attack.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says a non-joiner gives his rights 'to one who joined.' This sounds like he gives to a single person even though other joiners live there too, and that seems to be enough. That would go against רבה's rule that he must renounce to each one.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged him from a תנאי source

steps.confusionAlert: 'Two who did not join' giving to 'one who did not join' is a courtyard where nobody joined (see step 25). It works because after they give, he is the only resident left with rights, so nobody forbids him. Don't confuse this with the banned case of rights going to two non-joiners.

phrases.english: He raised an objection to him:
One who did not join the eiruv
gives his rights to one who joined,
phrases.notes: Key phrase for the challenge: 'to one.'

phrases.english: two who joined give their rights
to one who did not join,
and two who did not join give their rights
to two who joined,
or to one who did not join.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא continues in the next step.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that one must renounce to each resident
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא allows giving rights 'to one who joined,' which implies a single renunciation is enough even when other residents are present.

steps.title: The rest of the ברייתא: cases where giving up rights does not work
steps.stepSummary: אביי finishes quoting the ברייתא. It lists cases where giving up rights does not help, such as a joiner giving to a non-joiner, or two people giving to two non-joiners.
steps.simpleTranslation: But one who joined the עירוב may not give his rights to one who did not join. Two who joined may not give their rights to two who did not join. And two who did not join may not give their rights to two who did not join.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still inside the ברייתא that אביי started quoting in step 6. This is the second half, which lists the cases that do NOT work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half of the ברייתא (step 6) listed the cases that work. This half lists the cases that fail, because the giving does not end the problem of people forbidding each other. אביי's real attack comes from the first half, which he will go back to in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: But not. This opens the list of cases that do not work.
One who did not join the עירוב
Gives over his rights in the courtyard (ביטול רשות)

phrases.english: But not: one who joined the eiruv
giving his rights to one who did not join
and two who joined do not give their rights
to two who did not join
and two who did not join do not
give their rights to two who did not join
phrases.notes: This connects to steps 2-3. Two non-joiners cannot fix things by giving to each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל לֹא אֶחָד שֶׁעֵירַב נוֹתֵן רְשׁוּתוֹ לְאֶחָד שֶׁלֹּא עֵירַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the continuation of the ברייתא that אביי began quoting in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling (step 5) that the non-joiner must give up his rights to each resident
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This half finishes the source text. The attack itself is built from the first clause in the next steps.

steps.title: Looking closely at the first clause: who did the joiner join with?
steps.stepSummary: אביי goes back to the first clause, where a non-joiner gives to 'one who joined.' He asks what the case looks like. If the joiner were alone with the non-joiner, he would have had nobody to join with.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any event, the first clause teaches: one who did not join gives his rights to one who joined. What is the case? If there is no other person with him, then who did he join the עירוב with?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי is setting up his proof. He shows that the joiner in the first clause cannot be the only other person in the courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירוב needs at least two people joining together. So someone called 'one who joined' must have had a partner. That means the courtyard had at least two joiners plus the non-joiner.

keyTerms.meaning: In any event, it teaches. Used to focus on one part of a source for a proof.
The first clause of a source
What is the case? What does it look like?

phrases.english: In any event, the first clause teaches:
one who did not join
gives his rights to one who joined.
What is the case?
If there is no other person with him,
with whom did he join the eiruv?
phrases.notes: A person cannot make an עירוב by himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After quoting the whole ברייתא, אביי returns to its first clause to build his challenge.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He first shows that 'one who joined' requires a second joiner in the courtyard.

steps.title: So there were two joiners, and giving to one was still enough
steps.stepSummary: There must have been another joiner. Yet the ברייתא says the non-joiner gives to 'one who joined.' So giving to just one person is enough, which contradicts רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is obvious that there is another person with him. And still it says: 'to one who joined'!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי completes his challenge against רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There were at least two joiners, yet the non-joiner gave his rights to only one of them, and it worked. רבה had said he must give to each resident separately. The ברייתא seems to say the opposite.

phrases.english: Rather, it is obvious
that there is another person with him,
and yet it teaches: 'to one who joined'!
phrases.notes: The singular word 'one' is the heart of the attack.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This finishes the reasoning begun in step 8 and turns it into a direct contradiction.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that the forgetful resident must give up his rights to each and every resident
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There were two or more joiners, yet giving to only one worked. So giving to each person separately is not required.

steps.title: רבה's answer: the second joiner died
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that the ברייתא is a special case. There was a second joiner, but he died, so now only one joiner is left.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה? He can say: what case are we dealing with here? Where there was another person, and he died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how רבה defends his ruling against אביי's challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה agrees that the joiner must have had a partner when the עירוב was made. He says the partner died, so only one joiner is left now. Giving to that one person means giving to everyone, so רבה's rule still holds.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? Introduces a narrowing of the case.
There was someone, and he died

steps.whatToRemember: רבה holds that a forgetful resident must give up his rights to every resident. The ברייתא's 'to one who joined' is a case where the other joiner died, so only one remained.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבה is saying the עירוב was never valid. It was properly made with two people. Only now is one of them left.

phrases.english: And Rabba? (How does he explain this?)
What case are we dealing with here?
Where there was another person, and he died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This answers אביי's challenge from steps 8-9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the ברייתא is about a special situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to describe a courtyard with several joiners, where giving to one was enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: The second joiner died, so only one joiner is left. Giving to him is giving to everyone, and רבה's rule stands.

steps.title: The latter clause does not fit the 'he died' explanation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה's answer by looking at the last clause of the ברייתא. If the second joiner had died there too, the ruling in that clause would make no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the case is one where the other joiner was there and died, then look at the last clause: 'But one who joined may not give his rights to one who did not join.' If the other joiner died, why can't he?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבה's answer from Step 10. It points to the last clause of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last clause says a joiner cannot give his rights to a non-joiner. If his partner had died, only two people would be left in the courtyard: the joiner and the non-joiner. In that case giving up rights should work fine. So the last clause cannot be a 'he died' case.

keyTerms.meaning: There was one, and he died
Gives up his rights (to the courtyard)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two clauses. In the first clause a non-joiner gives his rights to a joiner, which works. In the last clause a joiner gives his rights to a non-joiner, which does not work.

phrases.english: If it is a case where there was another, and he died —
say the latter clause:
But one who joined in the eruv does not
give his rights to one who did not join.
And if it is a case where there was another and he died,
why not!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's explanation that the ברייתא deals with a case where the second joiner died.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the 'died' scenario applied, the last clause's ban on a joiner giving to a non-joiner would be pointless. With only two people left, giving up rights should work.

steps.title: So both clauses must involve a living second joiner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the last clause must deal with a living second joiner. Since the clauses go together, the first clause does too, which brings back the challenge to רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is obvious that the other joiner is there. And since in the last clause he is there, in the first clause he is there too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge. Both clauses must describe a courtyard where the second joiner is alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the last clause only makes sense if the partner is alive, the גמרא assumes the first clause has the same setup. But the first clause says a non-joiner gives his rights to 'one who joined.' That would mean giving to one joiner is enough even when two are present, which goes against רבה.

phrases.english: Rather, it is obvious that he is there.
And since in the latter clause he is there,
in the first clause too he is there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the challenge begun in Step 11 and applies it back to the first clause.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's view that a non-joiner must give his rights to every joiner.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The clauses of a ברייתא should share one setup. The last clause has a living partner, so the first clause does too, and there giving to one joiner is enough.

steps.title: Each clause can describe its own situation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that both clauses must share the same setup.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are these comparable? This one is as it is, and that one is as it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the challenge. The first clause can be a 'he died' case, while the last clause is a 'he is alive' case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge depended on assuming both clauses describe the same situation. The גמרא says there is no such rule here. Each clause deals with its own circumstances, so רבה's answer for the first clause still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this comparable? (Must they be the same?)
This one as it is, and that one as it is

phrases.english: Are they comparable?
This one as it is, and that one as it is.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reasoning of Step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the assumption that the first clause must match the last clause.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The challenge assumed every clause of the ברייתא shares one setup. In fact each clause can describe a different situation.

steps.title: Proof from the ברייתא: 'to two', not 'to one'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings support for רבה from the end of the first section of the ברייתא. Two non-joiners give their rights 'to two joiners,' which implies giving to only one is not enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is so, because the end of the first section teaches: 'And two who did not join give their rights to two who joined.' To two, yes. To one, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its rejection and supports רבה with a line from the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line describes two joiners who are both alive. It says the non-joiners give 'to two.' The exact wording implies that giving to just one of them would not work, which is exactly רבה's view. It also shows the ברייתא does switch between different situations.

keyTerms.meaning: The end of the first section
To two, yes; to one, no

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא does not disprove רבה. The 'to one who joined' line can be a case where the other joiner died, and the 'to two who joined' line shows that when both joiners are alive, rights must be given to both.
steps.whyThisMatters: It supports the practical rule that a non-joiner must give up his rights to every joiner present in the courtyard, not just to one of them.

phrases.english: Know this, for it teaches in the end of the first clause:
And two who did not join
give their rights to two who joined.
To two — yes! To one — no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rejection in Step 13 and confirms רבה's view.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's view that rights must be given to all joiners, and that the clauses of the ברייתא describe different situations.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's line: 'two who did not join give their rights to two who joined,' read as 'to two, yes; to one, no.'

steps.title: אביי reads 'to two' as 'to one of the two'
steps.stepSummary: אביי deflects the proof for רבה. He says 'to two joiners' really means giving rights to just one of the two.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אביי says: What does 'to two' mean? To one of the two.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the proof from the last step. He says the words 'to two' do not have to mean both of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof for רבה relied on the word 'to two': you must give your rights to both joiners. אביי reinterprets the word. It means giving your rights to one of the two joiners, and that one gift works for both. So the ברייתא does not prove that you must give to each person.

keyTerms.meaning: אביי, the אמורא who argues with רבה here

phrases.english: And Abaye says:
What is 'to two'?
To one of the two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought for רבה in step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The inference from the word 'to two'.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The phrase can mean 'one of the two,' so it does not prove that every joiner must receive the rights.

steps.title: Then the ברייתא should have said 'to one'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי: if that is the meaning, the ברייתא should simply have said 'to one'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let it teach: to one who joined, or to one who did not join.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks אביי's reading. If giving to one is enough, why does the ברייתא say 'two'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one joiner is all you need, the clearer wording would be 'to one who joined.' The fact that he joined already tells us a second person exists, because you cannot make an עירוב alone. So the word 'two' looks unnecessary under אביי's reading.

keyTerms.meaning: let it teach (it should have said)

phrases.english: If so, let it teach:
to one who joined the eruv
or to one who did not join.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's reinterpretation from step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's reading 'to one of the two'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If one is enough, the ברייתא should have said 'to one.' Writing 'two' suggests that both must receive the rights.

steps.title: The challenge to אביי stands
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא admits that the wording is a difficulty for אביי.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the question against אביי unanswered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'קשיא' means the wording problem stays open. It is a weakness in אביי's view, but it is not a full refutation that knocks his opinion out.
steps.confusionAlert: 'קשיא' here is not the same as 'תיובתא.' A תיובתא would fully refute אביי. Here his view still stands; it just has a difficulty.

phrases.english: It is difficult.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the challenge of step 16 without resolving it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: אביי's reading of 'to two' remains a difficulty, but it is not rejected.

steps.title: First clause of the ברייתא according to אביי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts going through the ברייתא's clauses. According to אביי, the first clause teaches that you don't need to give up rights to every single person.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who did not join gives his rights to one who joined. According to אביי, the other person is still there, and it teaches us that one need not give up rights to each and every person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains why each clause of the ברייתא is needed. It starts with the first clause and gives אביי's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For אביי, the second joiner is alive and present. The new lesson is that giving up rights to just one joiner is enough. You do not have to give up rights to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: gives up his rights in the courtyard
where he (the other person) is present
to give up one's rights (ביטול רשות)

phrases.english: One who did not join the eruv
gives his rights to one who joined.
According to Abaye, where the other one is present,
and it teaches us:
that one need not give up rights
to each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶחָד שֶׁלֹּא עֵירַב נוֹתֵן רְשׁוּתוֹ לְאֶחָד שֶׁעֵירַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new survey of each clause of the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to אביי, giving up rights to one joiner works even when another joiner is present.

steps.title: First clause of the ברייתא according to רבה
steps.stepSummary: According to רבה, the second joiner died. The lesson is that the רבנן did not make a decree out of worry about cases where he is still alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבה, there was another person and he died, and the רבנן did not decree because of times when he is present.
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא gives רבה's explanation of the same first clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבה, only one joiner is left, because the other one died. So this clause has to teach something else. The lesson is that we do not forbid this case out of fear that people will copy it when the second joiner is still alive. In that case, giving to one would not be enough.

phrases.english: According to Rabba, where there was another and he died,
and they did not decree because of times when he is present.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבה's parallel explanation of the clause from step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבה, the clause teaches that there is no גזירה against giving rights to the lone surviving joiner.

steps.title: Isn't the second clause obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says joiners may give their rights to a non-joiner. The גמרא asks why this needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: And two who joined give their rights to one who did not join. Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next clause of the ברייתא. It asks what new lesson the clause teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It seems clear that giving up rights can go in either direction. So the clause looks unnecessary, and the גמרא asks what it adds.

phrases.english: And two who joined the eruv give their rights
to one who did not join.
Isn't that obvious?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the second clause.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ruling seems self-evident, so the clause appears to teach nothing new.

steps.title: No penalty for the one who didn't join
steps.stepSummary: Without this clause, we might have thought the non-joiner is penalized and is not allowed to receive the rights.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: since he did not join, let us penalize him. So it teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'it's obvious' question by naming the mistake the clause prevents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think the non-joiner should be punished for not joining. The punishment would be that he must give up his rights to them, and they may not give their rights to him. The ברייתא teaches that there is no such penalty.

phrases.english: You might have said
since he did not join, let us penalize him,
it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: preventing a mistaken assumption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The non-joiner should be penalized and should not receive the joiners' rights.
steps.terutzMaskana: There is no penalty. Joiners may give their rights to a non-joiner.

steps.title: Third clause according to רבה: it explains the first clause
steps.stepSummary: For רבה, the last clause shows that you must give up rights to everyone. That proves the first clause is about a joiner who died.
steps.simpleTranslation: And two who did not join give their rights to two who joined. According to רבה, the end clause was taught to reveal the meaning of the first clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the third clause. It explains that for רבה, this clause is there to clarify the first clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last clause says rights go 'to two,' meaning to each joiner. So the first clause, which says rights go 'to one,' must be the special case where the second joiner died. This fits רבה's answer from step 10.

phrases.english: And two who did not join give their rights
to two who joined.
According to Rabba,
the end clause was taught to reveal the meaning of the first clause.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the third clause and explains its purpose for רבה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The end clause seems to repeat a known rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: It shows that the first clause must be a case where the second joiner died.

steps.title: Third clause according to אביי: no decree out of fear of mix-ups
steps.stepSummary: For אביי, the clause teaches that we do not forbid non-joiners from giving their rights to joiners out of fear that the joiners will give their rights the other way.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to אביי, the case of two who did not join was needed. You might have thought: let us decree, lest they come to give up rights to them. It teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why אביי needs the third clause, since for him it does not explain the first clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two people on each side, one might have expected the רבנן to forbid the whole arrangement. The worry would be that people mix up which side gives up rights to which. The ברייתא teaches that there is no such decree.

keyTerms.meaning: it would have entered your mind to say

steps.whatToRemember: Every clause of the ברייתא gets a purpose under both views. רבה reads the first clause as a case where the second joiner died. אביי reads it as teaching that giving up rights to one joiner is enough.

phrases.english: According to Abaye,
the case of two who did not join was necessary for him,
for it would have entered your mind to say:
let us decree, lest they come to give up rights to them.
It teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְאַבָּיֵי שְׁנַיִם שֶׁלֹּא עֵירְבוּ אִיצְטְרִיכָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives אביי's parallel explanation of the clause from step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: סלקא דעתך: preventing a mistaken assumption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן would forbid two non-joiners from giving rights to two joiners, out of fear the joiners would give rights the other way.
steps.terutzMaskana: There is no such decree; the arrangement is allowed.

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא add 'or to one who did not join'?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says rights may also be given to a non-joiner, and the גמרא asks why this extra line is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Or to one who did not join the עירוב.' Why do I need this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another line from the ברייתא and asks why it needs to be said. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already taught that people can give their rights to others. Adding 'or to one who did not join' seems obvious, since giving up rights is normally allowed. The גמרא wants to know what new point this line adds.

keyTerms.meaning: Or to one person who did not join the עירוב
Why do I need this? (a question about extra wording)

phrases.english: Or to one who did not join the eiruv.
Why do I need this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The clause 'or to one who did not join'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The clause seems unnecessary, since giving up rights is already known to be allowed.

steps.title: Even when nobody joined, there is no penalty
steps.stepSummary: We might have thought that if nobody in the courtyard joined, the רבנן would penalize them so people don't forget about עירוב. The ברייתא teaches that there is no such penalty.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: this only applies where some joined and some did not. But where none of them joined, we should penalize them so that the law of עירוב is not forgotten. So the ברייתא teaches us that it still works.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Without this line, we might think that when nobody made an עירוב, they lose the option of giving up rights as a penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that if a whole courtyard skips the עירוב and still fixes things through ביטול רשות, people will forget that an עירוב exists at all. The ברייתא tells us the רבנן did not make this penalty. Giving up rights works even when everyone failed to join.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces the mistaken assumption)
So that the law of עירוב is not forgotten

phrases.english: Lest you say:
These words apply where some of them joined
and some of them did not join.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הֵיכָא דְּכוּלָּן לֹא עֵירְבוּ — לִיקְנְסִינְהוּ,
phrases.english: But where none of them joined, let us penalize them,
so that the law of eiruv will not be forgotten,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: the clause rules out a possible penalty
steps.terutzHavaAmina: When nobody joined, they should be penalized and not allowed to give up rights.
steps.terutzMaskana: There is no penalty. Giving up rights works even when nobody joined.

steps.title: The ברייתא: a joiner cannot give his rights to a non-joiner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next clause: one who joined may not give his rights to one who did not join.
steps.simpleTranslation: But one who joined the עירוב may not give his rights to one who did not join.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the ברייתא. It is setting up the next move: seeing how אביי and רבה each understand this line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the first 'may not' clause in the ברייתא. The case is a courtyard where two people joined and one did not. One of the joiners tries to give his rights to the non-joiner, and the ברייתא says this does not work.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אֵין אֶחָד שֶׁעֵירַב נוֹתֵן רְשׁוּתוֹ
phrases.english: But one who joined may not give his rights
to one who did not join.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the ברייתא, now its 'may not' section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A joiner cannot give his rights to a non-joiner.

steps.title: אביי: this clause explains the earlier clause
steps.stepSummary: For אביי, this later clause was taught to make the meaning of the earlier clause clear, and it supports his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to אביי, the ברייתא taught the later clause to reveal the meaning of the first clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why this clause is needed according to אביי. For him, it is the key that shows how to read the earlier clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This clause forbids a joiner from giving his rights to a non-joiner. That only makes sense if his joining partner is still alive, because if the partner had died, only two people would be left and the giving would work. So the clause shows that the ברייתא is describing a living second joiner. For אביי, the first clause has the same setup, which proves that giving to one of the two joiners is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: It taught the last clause to reveal the meaning of the first clause

phrases.english: According to Abaye, it taught the latter clause
to reveal the meaning of the first clause,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the clause of step 26 using אביי's view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the clause is needed: it clarifies the earlier clause
steps.terutzMaskana: For אביי, this clause shows that rights can be given to one of two people.

steps.title: רבה: this clause is only there to match the earlier one
steps.stepSummary: For רבה, the clause adds no new law. It was written only to match the style of the first clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבה, since the ברייתא taught the first clause, it also taught the last clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains this clause according to רבה. For him, it teaches nothing new and was written only for parallel style.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה holds that you must give up your rights to everyone, so this line cannot be used as proof for אביי. By calling it a matching clause (אַיְּידֵי), רבה removes its force as evidence. This way his own reading of the earlier clause, about a joiner who died, stays in place.

keyTerms.term: אַיְּידֵי דִּתְנָא רֵישָׁא תְּנָא נָמֵי סֵיפָא
keyTerms.meaning: Since it taught the first clause, it also taught the last clause (just for matching style)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבה disagrees with the law in this clause. Both agree that a joiner cannot give to a non-joiner. They only argue about whether the clause proves anything about the earlier clause.
steps.whatToRemember: The same clause is real evidence for אביי but only a stylistic match for רבה. Their argument is about how to read the ברייתא, not about this law.

phrases.english: According to Rabba, since it taught the first clause
it also taught the latter clause.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְרַבָּה — אַיְּידֵי דִּתְנָא רֵישָׁא תְּנָא נָמֵי סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבה's different reading of the same clause discussed in step 27.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבה, no proof can be drawn from this clause.

steps.title: Why say that two joiners cannot give to two non-joiners?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says two joiners may not give their rights to two non-joiners, and the גמרא asks why this extra line is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And two who joined may not give their rights to two who did not join. Why do I need this too?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next clause and asks why it needs to be said. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know that a joiner cannot give his rights to a non-joiner. So it seems obvious that two joiners cannot give to two non-joiners. The word תּוּ ('further') stresses that this looks like plain repetition.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need this further statement?
Two people who joined the עירוב

phrases.english: And two who joined may not give their rights
to two who did not join.
Why do I need this further?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next 'may not' clause and asks why it is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The clause about two joiners and two non-joiners
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It seems to follow automatically from the clause in step 26.

steps.title: Case: one non-joiner then gives his rights to his friend
steps.stepSummary: The clause is needed for a case where one of the two non-joiners then gives up his rights to the other. That does not help, because when he gave them up he had no permission in the courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed where one of them gave up his rights to his friend. You might have said carrying should now be allowed. So it teaches us: since at the time he gave them up he had no permission in this courtyard, it does not work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the clause is about a special follow-up case. One of the two non-joiners tries to fix things by passing his rights to his friend.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We might think that once only one non-joiner is left, things are fixed and carrying is allowed. The ברייתא teaches that it is not allowed. When he gave up his rights, he himself had no permission (שַׁרְיוּתָא) in the courtyard, so his giving up does not help.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a specific case)

steps.whatToRemember: Giving up rights only helps if the giver had permission in the courtyard at the time he gave them up.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where one of them gave up his rights to his friend.
Lest you say: it should be permitted to him,
so it teaches us:
since at the time that he gave up his rights

phrases.aramaic: לָא הֲווֹ לֵיהּ שַׁרְיוּתָא בְּהָא חָצֵר — לָא.
phrases.english: he had no permission in this courtyard, it does not work.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: לא צריכא: a specific case is identified
steps.terutzHavaAmina: After one non-joiner gives up his rights to the other, carrying should be allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is not allowed, because the giver had no permission in the courtyard when he gave up his rights.

steps.title: Why say that two non-joiners cannot give to two non-joiners?
steps.stepSummary: The last clause says two non-joiners may not give their rights to two other non-joiners, and the גמרא asks why it is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And two who did not join may not give their rights to two who did not join. Why do I need this too?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last clause of the ברייתא and asks why it is needed. This sets up the final answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is obvious that giving rights to two non-joiners does not help, because two people without an עירוב are still left, and they still block each other. So the clause looks like it adds nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Two people who did not join the עירוב

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין שְׁנַיִם שֶׁלֹּא עֵירְבוּ נוֹתְנִין רְשׁוּתָן
phrases.english: And two who did not join may not give their rights
to two who did not join.
Why do I need this further?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same question as step 29, now on the last clause.
steps.kashyaTarget: The clause about two non-joiners giving to two non-joiners
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It is obvious that this cannot help, so the clause seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Case: 'acquire on condition to pass it on' does not work
steps.stepSummary: The clause is needed where the residents told one non-joiner to acquire their rights on condition that he pass them on to the other. This method does not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed where they said: 'Acquire our rights on condition that you pass them on.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the clause is about a clever workaround. The residents try to use one non-joiner as a middleman to pass all the rights to the other, and the ברייתא teaches that this fails.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plan is that one non-joiner receives everyone's rights and then hands them to his friend, leaving one person with all the rights. The ברייתא rules this out. The middleman himself is a non-joiner, so he cannot pass rights on the way the plan needs.

keyTerms.meaning: Acquire on condition that you transfer it onward

steps.whatToRemember: Each 'may not' clause in the ברייתא covers a specific workaround that fails: a joiner giving to a non-joiner, a non-joiner passing his rights to his friend, and using a middleman to pass rights on.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where they said: Acquire on condition to transfer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: לא צריכא: a specific case is identified
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Using one non-joiner as a middleman to pass all rights to the other should work.
steps.terutzMaskana: Using a middleman this way does not work.

steps.title: Can an heir give up rights in the courtyard?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רב נחמן whether an heir may do ביטול רשות in the courtyard in place of the person he inherited from.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked רב נחמן: An heir, what is the law? Can he give up his rights in the courtyard?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new question. רבא asks רב נחמן whether someone who inherits a courtyard home on שבת can give up the rights to it, the way the original owner could have.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case: a resident forgot to join the עירוב and died on שבת, so his share now belongs to his heir. The open question is whether the heir counts as the same person as the one who died, or as a new person whose rights only began on שבת. This sets up the answer and discussion that will follow.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him. This opens a real question of law, not an attack.
An heir, the person who inherits property after someone dies
What is the law? This opens a question where the answer is unknown.
That he gives up his rights in the courtyard so the others may carry

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a קשיא against anything. רבא is not attacking a source. He truly does not know the answer and is asking his teacher.
steps.whyThisMatters: It ties into the earlier idea in step 30: rights that come to someone only on שבת may not let him act. The question is whether an heir is like that, or whether he simply steps into the shoes of the one who died.

phrases.english: Rava asked of Rav Naḥman:
phrases.notes: Standard formula for a real question to a teacher.

phrases.english: An heir, what is the law, may he give up his rights?
phrases.notes: The case is where the owner, who had not joined the עירוב, died on שבת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתא's clauses are explained, the גמרא opens a new question on a related topic: ביטול רשות by someone whose rights came to him on שבת.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an heir who inherits on שבת may do ביטול רשות in place of the person who died. This depends on whether he counts as continuing that person or as someone who first gained rights on שבת.
